notes.b: Much of chemistry happens in solution, so you need exact words for the parts of one. Every later idea in this subsection, from concentration to dilution, is built on them.
points: A solution is a uniform (homogeneous) mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent. Uniform means it looks and behaves the same throughout, with no layers or visible particles.
The solute is the substance that dissolves, and the solvent is the substance it dissolves in. When the solvent is water the solution is called an aqueous solution.

notes.b: A solvent can only hold so much solute at a given temperature. The names unsaturated, saturated and supersaturated describe how close a solution is to that limit, or beyond it.
points: An unsaturated solution can still dissolve more solute at that temperature, so extra solute added to it simply dissolves.
A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at that temperature, with undissolved solid present. Any more solute added just sits at the bottom.
A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution holds at that temperature. It is unstable, which means it is easily upset and will not stay as it is.
A supersaturated solution is made by cooling a hot saturated solution carefully. A solid is usually more soluble when hot, so the cooled solution is left holding more than it normally could.

Adding a small seed crystal (a tiny crystal of the solute) to a supersaturated solution makes the excess solute crystallise suddenly, because the crystal gives the dissolved solute a surface to grow on.
Examples of solutes that form supersaturated solutions: sodium thiosulfate and sodium ethanoate.

notes.b: Saying a solution is strong or weak is not precise enough for chemistry. Concentration gives the amount of solute in a fixed volume, so it can be calculated with and compared.
points: Concentration is the amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution, usually in mol L⁻¹ (molarity, M, meaning moles of solute per litre) or g L⁻¹ (grams of solute per litre).
Concentration (mol L⁻¹) = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution in litres, so c = n ÷ V and n = c × V. Remember that the volume is that of the whole solution, not just the solvent.

Model: the same number of solute particles in a smaller volume gives a higher concentration, because the particles are packed more closely. Diluting spreads the same particles through a larger volume.
A standard solution is a solution whose concentration is accurately known. It is the starting point for finding the concentrations of other solutions.
notes.tip: Concentration is per litre of solution, not per litre of solvent. Use the final volume of the made-up solution in c = n ÷ V.

notes.h: Worked examples: concentration and mass needed
notes.b: Two calculations cover most questions on this topic. One finds the concentration from a mass of solute, and the other works backwards from a concentration to the mass to weigh out. Convert cm³ to litres first by dividing by 1000.
points: Finding a concentration: 5.30 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃, M = 106 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved. Anhydrous means it has no water of crystallisation. Moles: n = 5.30 ÷ 106 = 0.0500 mol.
The 0.0500 mol is made up to 500 cm³ (0.500 L). Then c = 0.0500 ÷ 0.500 = 0.100 mol L⁻¹.
Finding a mass needed: for 250 cm³ of 0.100 M sodium hydroxide (M = 40 g mol⁻¹), first find the moles from n = c × V = 0.100 × 0.250 = 0.0250 mol.
Then change moles to mass by multiplying by the molar mass (the mass of one mole): m = 0.0250 × 40 = 1.00 g.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to calculate concentrations and masses. Show each step: the relationship, the numbers with units, then the answer.

notes.h: Primary standards: what they are and their properties
notes.b: To make a standard solution by weighing, you must trust the mass on the balance to be the true amount of the substance. Only certain substances are reliable enough, and they are called primary standards.
points: A primary standard is a substance that can be weighed out accurately to make a standard solution directly.
A primary standard is available in a very pure state, so the mass weighed is all the substance and not impurities.
A primary standard is stable in air: it does not absorb water or carbon dioxide, or react with oxygen. If it did, its mass would change while being weighed.
A primary standard has a known formula, so its molar mass and the moles weighed out can be calculated, and it dissolves readily in water.
A primary standard preferably has a high molar mass, which reduces weighing errors. A larger mass is needed for each mole, so a small error on the balance is a smaller fraction of the whole.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to give properties of a primary standard. Give several, each with its reason.

notes.h: Primary standards: examples and substances that are not
notes.b: Which substance you choose depends on the type of titration (a method that reacts measured volumes of two solutions to find an unknown concentration). Some familiar laboratory chemicals fail the tests for a primary standard.
points: Anhydrous sodium carbonate is a primary standard used in acid–base titrations (reactions between an acid and a base).
Ammonium iron(II) sulfate, (NH₄)₂Fe(SO₄)₂·6H₂O, dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid, is a primary standard for redox titrations (reactions involving the transfer of electrons).
Sodium hydroxide is not a primary standard because it absorbs water and carbon dioxide from the air, so its mass is not the true mass of sodium hydroxide.
Hydrochloric acid is not a primary standard because its concentration changes as HCl evaporates.
Solutions of sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid are standardised, meaning their exact concentration is found, by titration against a primary standard.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain why sodium hydroxide is not a primary standard. Say that it absorbs water and carbon dioxide from the air.

notes.h: Preparing a standard solution: the method
notes.b: Making a standard solution from a weighed primary standard is an investigation with a fixed method. The aim is a solution of accurately known concentration, here 250 cm³ in a volumetric flask (a flask with a single mark showing an exact volume).
points: 1. Weigh accurately (to 0.01 g or better) the calculated mass of the primary standard on a clock glass or weighing boat.
2. Transfer the solid to a beaker, and rinse the clock glass into the beaker with deionised water from a wash bottle, so that none of the weighed solid is left behind.
3. Dissolve the solid in a small volume of deionised water, stirring with a glass rod.
4. Pour the solution through a funnel into a volumetric flask of the required volume, e.g. 250 cm³.
5. Rinse the beaker, glass rod and funnel into the flask with deionised water so that no solute is lost.

6. Add deionised water until the flask is near the mark, then add the last drops with a dropper until the bottom of the meniscus (the curved surface of the liquid) sits on the graduation mark, viewed at eye level.
7. Stopper the flask and invert it about 20 times so the solution is uniform.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to describe how to make up a standard solution of sodium carbonate. Give the steps in order, starting with the mass calculated for the volume and concentration required.

notes.h: Preparing a standard solution: glassware, precision and diagrams
notes.b: The choice of glassware decides how accurate the final concentration is. Examiners also expect labelled diagrams of the apparatus in the method.
points: Precision and accuracy: the volumetric flask holds an accurately known volume, whereas a beaker or measuring cylinder is not accurate enough.
Diagram: a volumetric flask with its graduation mark, and the meniscus shown at eye level.
Diagram: a funnel in the neck of the volumetric flask during the transfer.
Diagram: a beaker with a glass rod stirring the dissolving solid.

notes.b: A concentrated solution can be turned into a weaker one by adding solvent. The solute is not changed, only spread through more volume, which gives a simple equation to use.
points: Diluting adds solvent, so the number of moles of solute stays the same. This gives c₁V₁ = c₂V₂, where c₁ and V₁ are the original solution and c₂ and V₂ the diluted one.
Example: to make 250 cm³ of 0.10 M HCl from 1.0 M HCl, V₁ = (0.10 × 250) ÷ 1.0 = 25 cm³.
Pipette 25 cm³ of the 1.0 M acid into a 250 cm³ volumetric flask and make up to the mark with water.
Use a pipette (a glass tube that measures one exact volume), with a pipette filler to draw up the liquid, for the volume of the original solution, and a volumetric flask for the final volume.
Diagram: a pipette with a pipette filler, filled to the graduation mark.
notes.tip: In dilution the moles stay the same and only the volume changes. Exams ask for dilution calculations, so state c₁V₁ = c₂V₂ and substitute.

notes.b: Sometimes a whole range of concentrations is needed, such as for a set of test solutions. Rather than diluting from the stock solution every time, you dilute step by step.
points: Serial dilution is a series of dilutions, each using the previous solution, usually by the same factor.
Example: starting from 1.0 M, take 10 cm³ and make it up to 100 cm³ to give 0.10 M. Repeating from that solution gives 0.010 M and then 0.0010 M.
Serial dilution is used to make a range of concentrations accurately.

notes.b: Concentration can be expressed in several ways depending on the substance and the use. Each unit says how much solute is present in a fixed amount of solution or mixture.
points: mol L⁻¹ (molarity, M): moles of solute per litre of solution.
g L⁻¹: grams of solute per litre of solution.
%w/v (weight per volume): grams of solute per 100 cm³ of solution. For example, 5% w/v glucose contains 5 g per 100 cm³.
%v/v (volume per volume): cm³ of solute per 100 cm³ of solution, used for a liquid dissolved in a liquid. For example, wine labelled 12% v/v contains 12 cm³ of ethanol in every 100 cm³.
%w/w (weight per weight): grams of solute per 100 g of the whole mixture, used for solids and creams. For example, 1% w/w hydrocortisone cream has 1 g in every 100 g.
notes.tip: %w/v is per 100 cm³ of solution, not per litre.

notes.h: Converting between mol L⁻¹, g L⁻¹ and %w/v
notes.b: The molar mass links moles to grams, and the fact that 100 cm³ is one-tenth of a litre links g L⁻¹ to %w/v. Between them you can move from any one of these units to any other.
points: mol L⁻¹ to g L⁻¹: multiply by the molar mass. Example: 0.10 M NaOH × 40 g mol⁻¹ = 4.0 g L⁻¹.
g L⁻¹ to mol L⁻¹: divide by the molar mass. Example: 9.8 g L⁻¹ of H₂SO₄ ÷ 98 g mol⁻¹ = 0.10 mol L⁻¹.
g L⁻¹ to %w/v: divide by 10, since 100 cm³ is one-tenth of a litre. Example: 4.0 g L⁻¹ = 0.40% w/v.
To reverse the step, multiply %w/v by 10 to get g L⁻¹.
%w/v to mol L⁻¹: multiply by 10 to get g L⁻¹, then divide by the molar mass. Example: 0.9% w/v physiological saline (NaCl, M = 58.5 g mol⁻¹): 0.9 × 10 = 9.0 g L⁻¹.
Then 9.0 g L⁻¹ ÷ 58.5 g mol⁻¹ = 0.15 mol L⁻¹.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to convert a concentration in mol L⁻¹ to g L⁻¹ or %w/v and back. Remember that %w/v is per 100 cm³, so the factor is 10, not 1000.

notes.h: Converting %v/v and %w/w to volume and mass
notes.b: Percentages for liquids and creams tell you how much of the active substance is in a given amount of the product. These calculations turn the percentage back into an actual volume or mass.
points: %v/v to volume: volume of solute = volume of solution × %v/v ÷ 100.
Example: ethanol in 750 cm³ of 12% v/v wine = 750 × 12 ÷ 100 = 90 cm³.
%v/v to mass, using density (the mass of each cm³ of the substance): mass = volume × density.
Example: 90 cm³ of ethanol × 0.789 g cm⁻³ = 71 g.
%w/w to mass: mass of solute = mass of mixture × %w/w ÷ 100.
Example: 30 g of a 1% w/w cream contains 30 × 1 ÷ 100 = 0.30 g of the active ingredient.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to calculate the volume of alcohol in a drink from its %v/v. Multiply the volume of the drink by the percentage and divide by 100.

notes.b: Some solutions are so dilute that mol L⁻¹ gives very tiny numbers. Parts per million is a convenient unit for these, and it is used for pollutants and similar substances.
points: p.p.m. (parts per million) is the number of parts of solute in one million parts of solution or mixture. It is used for very dilute solutions, such as pollutants and dissolved substances in water.
For dilute aqueous solutions, 1 p.p.m. = 1 mg of solute per litre of solution (1 mg L⁻¹). This holds because 1 L of water has a mass of about 1 kg, which is 10⁶ mg.
For solids, 1 p.p.m. = 1 mg per kg.
Example: 0.0050 g of a substance in 2.5 L of water. First 0.0050 g = 5.0 mg. Then 5.0 mg ÷ 2.5 L = 2.0 p.p.m.
Example: 1.0 mg L⁻¹ of fluoride is 1.0 p.p.m. Fluoridated water in Ireland is about 0.6–0.8 p.p.m. (mg L⁻¹).
p.p.m. to mol L⁻¹: convert to g L⁻¹ first, e.g. 2.0 p.p.m. = 2.0 mg L⁻¹ = 0.0020 g L⁻¹, then divide by the molar mass.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to express a concentration in p.p.m. Remember that p.p.m. equal to mg L⁻¹ holds only for dilute aqueous solutions.

keyTerms.definition: A uniform mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent.
The substance that dissolves in a solvent to form a solution.
The substance in which a solute dissolves; water in an aqueous solution.
The amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution, usually in mol L⁻¹ or g L⁻¹.
A solution that contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at that temperature, with undissolved solid present.
A solution containing more dissolved solute than a saturated solution holds at that temperature; it is unstable.
A solution whose concentration is accurately known.
A pure, stable substance of known formula that can be weighed out accurately to make a standard solution directly.
A flask that holds an accurately known volume when filled to its graduation mark.
Reducing a solution's concentration by adding solvent, which keeps the number of moles of solute the same.
A series of dilutions, each made from the previous solution, usually by the same factor.
Moles of solute per litre of solution.
Grams of solute per litre of solution.
Grams of solute per 100 cm³ of solution.
Volume of solute in cm³ per 100 cm³ of solution, used for a liquid in a liquid.
Grams of solute per 100 g of the whole mixture, used for solids and creams.
A solution of 0.9% w/v sodium chloride, NaCl.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would prepare 250 cm³ of a 0.100 M standard solution of anhydrous sodium carbonate, including the mass needed.
questions.model: Mass needed: M(Na₂CO₃) = 106 g mol⁻¹. Moles: n = c × V = 0.100 × 0.250 = 0.0250 mol. Mass: m = n × M = 0.0250 × 106 = 2.65 g. Method: weigh 2.65 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate accurately to 0.01 g on a clock glass or weighing boat. Transfer it to a beaker, rinsing the clock glass into the beaker with deionised water from a wash bottle. Dissolve the solid in a small volume of deionised water, stirring with a glass rod. Pour the solution through a funnel into a 250 cm³ volumetric flask, then rinse the beaker, rod and funnel into the flask with deionised water. Add deionised water until near the mark, then add the last drops with a dropper until the bottom of the meniscus sits on the graduation mark at eye level. Stopper the flask and invert it about 20 times to make the solution uniform.

questions.prompt: State three properties of a primary standard and explain why sodium hydroxide is not used as one.
questions.model: Three properties of a primary standard: it is available in a very pure state; it is stable in air (it does not absorb water or carbon dioxide, or react with oxygen); it has a known formula, dissolves readily in water and preferably has a high molar mass. Sodium hydroxide is not a primary standard because it absorbs water and carbon dioxide from the air, so the mass weighed out does not give an accurately known amount of sodium hydroxide.

questions.prompt: What volume of 2.0 M sulfuric acid is needed to make 500 cm³ of 0.10 M sulfuric acid?
questions.model: Dilution keeps the moles of solute the same, so c₁V₁ = c₂V₂. Substitute c₁ = 2.0 mol L⁻¹, c₂ = 0.10 mol L⁻¹ and V₂ = 500 cm³: 2.0 × V₁ = 0.10 × 500 = 50, so V₁ = 50 ÷ 2.0 = 25 cm³. Pipette 25 cm³ of the 2.0 M acid into a 500 cm³ volumetric flask and make up to the mark with water.

questions.prompt: A solution of sodium hydroxide has a concentration of 0.25 mol L⁻¹. Express its concentration in (i) g L⁻¹, (ii) %w/v.
questions.model: (i) M(NaOH) = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g mol⁻¹. Mass concentration: 0.25 mol L⁻¹ × 40 g mol⁻¹ = 10 g L⁻¹. (ii) 10 g L⁻¹ ÷ 10 = 1.0 g per 100 cm³, so the concentration is 1.0% w/v.

questions.prompt: Calculate the volume of ethanol in a 500 cm³ bottle of beer that is 4.5% v/v.
questions.model: Volume of solute = volume of solution × %v/v ÷ 100 = 500 × 4.5 ÷ 100 = 22.5 cm³ of ethanol.

questions.prompt: A 250 cm³ water sample contains 0.40 mg of nitrate ions. Express this concentration in p.p.m.
questions.model: Convert the volume to litres: 250 cm³ = 0.250 L. Concentration in mg L⁻¹: 0.40 mg ÷ 0.250 L = 1.6 mg L⁻¹. For a dilute aqueous solution, 1 p.p.m. = 1 mg L⁻¹, so the concentration is 1.6 p.p.m.
